newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ING RULES OUT BARINGS SHARE COMPENSATION.
newsitem.headline: ING RULES OUT BARINGS SHARE COMPENSATION.

text.p: Dutch financial services group ING Groep NV (ING) said on Tuesday it had no intention of paying compensation to preference shareholders in Barings, the British merchant bank ING bought from collapse in March 1995.

Executive board chairman Aad Jacobs told the annual meeting of ING shareholders that ING decided not to pay for the ordinary and preference shares and part of the subordinated bonds when it bought the British bank for 1.7 billion guilders.
He said the collapse of Barings from losses caused by unauthorised derivatives trading in Singapore "had nothing to do" with the Dutch group.
"I can't pay the Barings shareholders and I'm not going to," Jacobs told the meeting.
He was responding to a question from a shareholder, who said the holders of 50 million stg of preference shares paying an annual dividend of five million stg had lost everything.
They were mainly pensioners and small investors who sought to augment their income with dividends from an investment they thought was risk free, he said.
The shareholder said most Barings staff kept their jobs, Barings bondholders were likely to receive compensation and 10 million stg was paid to shareholder the Barings Foundation.

He asked if anything could be done to help the preference shareholders, such as making a nominal payment to them. "They ...appear to be the only party to get nothing back and I suspect are the most deserving to receive something," he said.
But Jacobs said shareholders ran a certain amount of risk and ING was not obliged to compensate them for their losses.
He said ING made a payment "in the name of humanity" to the Barings Foundation, as it helped disabled people.
ING supervisory board chairman Mijnderd Ververs said: "You have to accept this as a fact of life."
